n: A new heading begins Isaiah’s next prophecy (chapters 2–4). Isaiah 2–14 is quoted almost entirely by Nephi in 2 Nephi 12–24, with some meaningful differences.

f.w: The word that Isaiah the son of Amoz saw

n: In the last days the Lord’s temple will be raised up like the highest mountain, and people from every nation will stream to it. Latter-day Saints see this fulfilled in the gathering to temples and in the Salt Lake Temple set among the Rocky Mountains.

f.w: the mountain of the LORD's house
f.g: The temple; mountains were seen as meeting places between God and people (Exodus 19:20).
Stream like a river — but uphill, a miracle of gathering.

n: People invite one another to go to the Lord’s house to learn His ways and walk in His paths. Latter-day prophets have taught that God’s word will go forth from two centers, Zion and Jerusalem.

f.w: he will teach us of his ways
out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem

n: When the Lord reigns, He will settle disputes among nations, and people will turn weapons into farming tools. This describes the peace of the Millennium.

f.w: neither shall they learn war any more

n: Isaiah invites his own people, Israel, to walk in God’s light now. 2 Nephi 12:5 adds: “yea, come, for ye have all gone astray, every one to his wicked ways.”

f.w: walk in the light of the LORD

n: Isaiah turns to present problems: God has let His people go because they have filled the land with eastern fortune-telling and Philistine-style magic and made alliances with foreigners.

f.g: Filled with customs and divination from the east (Syria, Mesopotamia).

f.w: please themselves in the children of strangers

n: Judah has grown wealthy and militarily strong under kings like Uzziah. But the law warned kings not to trust in gold or horses.
Their land is also full of idols. People bow to things their own hands made — the irony Isaiah mocks again later (44:9-20).

Everyone, common and important alike, bows to idols. The KJV reads that people bow down; 2 Nephi 12:9 reads that the mean man “boweth not down” and the great man “humbleth himself not” — they will not humble themselves before God.
Isaiah tells them to hide among the rocks out of fear of the Lord’s glorious majesty. The Book of Mormon version begins, “O ye wicked ones,” making clear who must hide.
Proud human looks will be brought low, and the Lord alone will be lifted up on that day. This refrain repeats in verse 17.

f.g: A phrase pointing to the day of the Lord — His judgment and Second Coming.

n: The day of the Lord will come against everything proud and lofty. 2 Nephi 12:12 adds that this day “soon cometh upon all nations,” widening its scope.
Even the tallest cedars of Lebanon and the mighty oaks of Bashan — symbols of proud strength — will be humbled.

f.g: Fertile land east of the Sea of Galilee, famous for oaks and cattle.

n: High mountains and hills, symbols of human pride, will be brought low. 2 Nephi adds “upon all the nations which are lifted up, and upon every people.”
Every tall tower and fortified wall — things people trust for safety — will fall.

Even great trading ships and beautiful luxury goods will be humbled. 2 Nephi 12:16 reads “upon all the ships of the sea, and upon all the ships of Tarshish” — the first phrase matches the ancient Greek Septuagint, and the second the Hebrew.

f.g: Large ocean-going merchant ships; Tarshish was a distant port, possibly in Spain.

n: The refrain returns: human pride will be bowed down and the Lord alone exalted.

f.w: the LORD alone shall be exalted

n: God will completely wipe out idols. This short verse stands alone for emphasis.
People will flee into caves and holes in the rocks when the Lord rises to shake the earth. The Second Coming is described with great earthquakes in latter-day scripture.
In that day people will throw their silver and gold idols to the moles and bats — creatures of darkness — because they will see how worthless idols are.

f.w: to the moles and to the bats
f.g: Unclean creatures living in dark holes — the idols are tossed into the dirt.

n: They will hide in cracks of rocks and on jagged cliffs, terrified of the Lord’s majesty as He shakes the earth.
Stop trusting in mere mortals whose life is only a breath. Why rely on someone so fragile instead of God?

f.w: whose breath is in his nostrils
